title: Lock, stock and two missing grandmas
gist: Resolution Foundation's weekly roundup backs ending the UK triple lock ratchet (as Burnham proposes for a National Care Service), and flags that a frozen benefit cap capped ~36,000 more households with children after the two child limit was removed. It also covers one-in-six people using AI chatbots for legal problems, France's rust belt revived by Luxembourg commuting, and worsening generational health.

themes.theme: UK pensions triple lock reform and care funding

insights.claim: The UK is moving closer to ending the State Pension triple lock 'ratchet', with the Resolution Foundation backing a switch to pensions keeping pace with earnings growth.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Ending the ratchet would lower the long-run growth path of the UK's largest welfare outlay, easing gilt-supply and fiscal-rule pressure over time.
insights.quote: the State Pension should keep pace with earnings growth, but good riddance to the ratchet!
insights.locator: This week, we got a step

insights.claim: Burnham has proposed ending the triple lock ratchet and redirecting the savings into a National Care Service.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Signals a political trade-off of pension generosity for social care spending — a reallocation rather than a net fiscal saving.
insights.quote: Burnham’s big, bold plan to end the triple lock ratchet and pour the savings into a National Care Service

insights.claim: UK residential care costs between £1,000 and £1,400 a week, and even the poorest, lowest-saving couples receiving the most state support still pay around £9,000 a year in 'user charges', according to a Joseph Roundtree Foundation briefing.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: The scale of out-of-pocket care costs underpins political momentum for a National Care Service, implying rising public care spending and pressure on care-home provider economics.
insights.quote: Residential care costs between £1,000 and £1,400 a week.

insights.claim: Low-income care residents pay only slightly less than high-income equivalents, which Dan Neidle has likened to an arbitrary tax handed out by lottery; free personal care would help but not fix all problems.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Regressivity of current care charges strengthens the case for reform; free personal care is framed as a partial fix.
insights.quote: likened the whole thing to an arbitrary tax handed out by lottery

insights.claim: The UK Budget is due on the 28th, with cost-of-living concerns central to what the Chancellor must address.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Fiscal event risk for UK assets this month; cost-of-living measures likely a focus.
insights.locator: We’ve also officially entered Budget month.

insights.claim: Around one-in-six people with a legal problem have used an AI chatbot for help, per a survey of 3,000 people who had a legal problem.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Shows real-world consumer adoption of generative AI in professional-services substitution, a threat to low-end legal advice revenue.
insights.quote: around one-in-six people with a legal problem have turned to an AI chatbot for help
insights.locator: You’ll be hearing from my chat bot.

insights.claim: AI legal-help use skews young: 26% of 18-24-year-olds with a legal problem used a chatbot versus 10% of 55-64-year-olds.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Generational adoption gradient implies AI legal-advice usage will grow as younger cohorts age.
insights.locator: You’ll be hearing from my chat bot.

insights.claim: Chatbot legal use spans consumer disputes, landlord-tenant rows, employment and family law — areas largely outside legal aid scope.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: AI is filling an unmet-need gap left by the state rather than only displacing paid lawyers.
insights.quote: common, stressful, and often difficult to navigate without advice, but that largely fall outside the scope of legal aid
insights.locator: You’ll be hearing from my chat bot.

insights.claim: AI legal advice could either make justice far more accessible (if accurate) or clog public services with occasionally spurious complaints and appeals.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A second-order risk: AI-lowered friction could raise caseloads and administrative costs for tribunals and public bodies.
insights.quote: Or our public services may get irreparably gummed up with (occasionally spurious) complaints and appeals.
insights.locator: You’ll be hearing from my chat bot.

themes.theme: Delayed fertility and the shrinking grandparent generation

insights.claim: In the US, median age at first grandmotherhood rose from 44 under 1960 birth patterns to 57 in 2024, cutting the average healthy years shared with grandchildren by nearly half.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Compounding childbearing delays reduce informal childcare supply from grandparents, with knock-on effects for parental labour supply and demand for paid childcare.
insights.quote: median age at first grandmotherhood shot up from 44 under 1960 birth patterns to 57 in 2024

insights.claim: Resolution Foundation pushes back on the 'Rotten Adult Kid' framing, attributing fertility decline to a 'relationship recession', financial constraints and housing costs rather than insufficient pressure from would-be grandparents.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Locates fertility decline in housing and affordability — implying policy levers (housing supply, costs) matter for demographics.
insights.quote: a ‘relationship recession’, financial constraints and housing costs

themes.theme: Regional renewal: France's rust belt revived by Luxembourg

insights.claim: France's rust belt lost 400,000 manufacturing jobs between 1975 and the late 2010s, but was revived by booming neighbour Luxembourg; by 2021 over a third of prime-age workers in border towns commuted across, earning 60-65% more than comparable French workers.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Proximity to a high-productivity hub can rescue deindustrialised regions via commuting, not reindustrialisation.
insights.quote: By 2021, over a third of prime-age workers in border towns commuted across, earning 60 to 65 per cent more

insights.claim: 60% of the rise in cross-border employment from France's rust belt was in services; employment rates rose 7 percentage points, population grew 15%, benefits reliance fell, and rents rose by around a third.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Service-led renewal drives local housing demand and rents — the 'usual price' of a booming local economy.
insights.quote: 60 per cent of the increase in cross-border employment driven by services

insights.claim: Far-right and anti-EU voting fell in the revived French border regions relative to similar regions, suggesting deindustrialised areas are not doomed to anti-globalisation backlash.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Economic revival can reduce populist political risk — relevant for assessing political stability in left-behind regions.
insights.quote: are not inherently rigid nor doomed to fall to anti-globalization backlash, but can and do adjust

insights.claim: The Resolution Foundation argues that a 'new age of industrialisation' may not be the only, or even the most effective, way to raise UK regional living standards; agglomeration and services offer an alternative.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Challenges industrial-policy-led regional strategy; favours city agglomeration and service-sector growth.
insights.quote: a ‘new age of industrialisation’ is not the only, or even the most effective, way to boost living standards

insights.claim: Younger generations appear to be seeing worsening health ('generational health drift'): US 1950s-born cohorts saw worsening mortality across most of their lives, and cohorts born twenty years later saw rising deaths in their 30s and early 40s.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption of steady longevity gains, with implications for pension, insurance and health-system planning.

insights.claim: In the UK, diabetes among people in their 40s almost doubled from 3.1% among Baby Boomers to 5.9% among Gen X, while Gen Z have the highest childhood obesity rates.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Rising chronic disease prevalence signals growing structural demand for metabolic/diabetes care and pressure on the NHS.
insights.quote: diabetes among 40-somethings almost doubled, from 3.1 per cent among Baby Boomers to 5.9 per cent among Gen X

insights.claim: Younger generations reaching retirement age in worse health could magnify the fiscal and societal costs of population ageing.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Adds upside risk to long-run health and disability spending projections.

themes.theme: UK benefit cap and child poverty

insights.claim: The UK benefit cap has not been uprated since 2023, so every increase in benefit rates (e.g. the April 2024 LHA uprating) pushes more households onto the cap.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A frozen cap acts as a stealth fiscal drag, clawing back the value of benefit increases.
insights.quote: the value of the cap hasn’t changed since 2023

insights.claim: The removal of the two child limit in April will mean 425,000 fewer children in poverty by the end of the decade, but it caused a steep rise in capped households.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Policy interactions blunt the poverty impact of the two child limit removal.
insights.quote: there will be 425,000 fewer children living in poverty by the end of the decade

insights.claim: Around 36,000 more households with children were capped this April, a 37% increase in capped households with children, cutting them off from the boost of ending the two child limit.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Signals the next likely target for UK child-poverty policy and an additional fiscal cost if the cap is reformed.
insights.quote: a 37 per cent increase in the number of capped households with children

insights.claim: The Resolution Foundation argues the benefit cap, like the two child limit, arbitrarily breaks the link between needs and entitlement and any government serious about child poverty should review it; Scottish councils already offset it.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Raises probability of benefit cap reform being pressed in the Budget debate.
insights.quote: any UK government wanting to do more to reduce child poverty should look hard at this capricious cap
